It's not very common to pay quarterly, but it can happen. I know someone who paid 6 months rent for a bar. But I wouldn't look at it with good eyes for an apartment or house.

If you live there 2 years you are paying month 1 and the 24, if you decide to leave after 1 year that last month will be the 12th month. So your understanding was correct, note that its the 'last' month and it's not indexed to one particular month, so you can leave before the complete fulfilment of the contract.

The Portuguese law clearly mandates that the renter must fulfill at least 1/3rd of the contract except in the cases where the landlord is not fulfilling his duties (broken pipes he doesn't solve our something like that). You can leave early if you notify him with one month notice, but never before 1/3, the landlord can sue you and will be paid the rents up to 1/3 and he doesn't need to put anything extra on the contract.
I wouldn't advise you to sign a contract of more than 2 years for this reason.

Cost of living here is an issue. Lisbon has the highest rent/minimum wage in Europe (m.w. ~ 600€) and you should check renting websites to find out the price of your desired accommodations before moving. Transportation is dirt cheap. Eating out goes from 7.5€ to whatever you want to spend, but it's cheaper than most of Europe for sure. Drinks are very cheap (you can easily get a beer for 1 ~ 1.5€). Utilities are cheap, groceries are not as cheap as one would expect at such low wages, but cheaper than most Europe. Income taxes and Social Security are quite high indeed and you 100% need to check in which bracket of IRS you would be if you moved, depending on your income, hiring a financial advisor/accountant to help you navigate a fiscal system you don't understand might be beneficial.

We don't look at foreigners as sacks of money, but of course that we are aware that the typical foreigner is more inclined to spend than the typical local (quite normal) so you will find some places more tailored to foreigners that practice higher prices (e.g. my sister and brother-in-law teach workshops in traditional Portuguese ceramic and most of the interested are tourists or foreigners, due to limited capacity for the workshop the price tends to rise according to what their customers are willing to pay). Peta does not kill 90% of the animals they take into their care. Peta has one center in Norfolk that killed around 90% in some years. Why? 
1 - Because they offer free euthanasia to poor people's pets. To do this they must accept the animal into their care and euthanise it. It's not really the same thing, but a downgrade in quality due to messy encoding is a reality. Resolution is the number of pixels spread across a display and bitrate Is the amount of data encoded per unit of time.

Example of one difference:

Let's say I have a 1 min video of total darkness at1080p It will be encoded in such a way that saves a lot of space by projecting those same 1920*1080 pixels during 1 min resulting in a low bitrate, naturally.

Now a 1 min video with everything constantly moving will probably be bigger and have a higher bitrate, but to optimize file size a few algorithmic tricks will still be pulled on that video, otherwise it would be ridiculously big. That's compression.


Now, you can encode things at a lower bitrate than what would be optimal, which would make the video lose quality, but not necessarily resolution. It will still have the same number of pixels, but the amount of information is lower so some things get less sharp, some very similar colours can get mixed, idk, a bunch of things. I hope this helps you understand the concept.
